title: Google Docs
summary: Real-time collaborative editing: clients send operations over WebSockets to a per-document server that orders and transforms them (OT), or merge-friendly CRDTs reconcile edits without a central order.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: Many users edit the same document concurrently; see each other's changes and cursors live
Offline edits merge on reconnect; version history and restore
Remote edits visible < 200 ms; local typing never waits on the network
All replicas converge to the same document (no lost keystrokes)
Up to ~100 concurrent editors per doc; billions of docs

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Load per document is tiny; the challenge is correctness — making concurrent edits converge — and routing all editors of a doc to the same place.

head: Data
Key
Notes
rows: Every N ops so loading doesn't replay everything
Anchored to positions that are transformed with edits

blocks.caption: All editors of one document meet at one document session server

items: Client applies the edit locally at once, then sends the op with the revision it was based on.
The session server (one owner per doc, via consistent hashing or a lease) transforms the op against ops committed since `baseRev`.
It appends to the op log, assigns rev N, acks the author and broadcasts the transformed op to others.
Clients transform incoming ops against their own unacknowledged ops before applying.

blocks.text:
Doc: "abc"
Alice: insert 'X' at 1  ->  "aXbc"
Bob:   delete at 2      ->  "ab"   (removes 'c')
Server receives Alice first (rev 1). Bob's op was based on rev 0:
transform(delete@2, against insert@1) = delete@3
Result everywhere: "aXb"

items: Server is the single source of order, so OT only needs transform against concurrent ops — simpler than peer-to-peer OT.
Client keeps one in-flight op and buffers the rest (Jupiter / Google Wave model), reducing transform complexity.
Cursors and comment anchors are transformed like positions.

sections.title: Deep dive: CRDTs as the alternative

cols.title: OT (Google Docs)
cons: Transform functions are hard to get right

cols.title: CRDT (Yjs, Automerge)
pros: No central order needed; works peer-to-peer and offline

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: With a server in the loop anyway, OT is a solid choice; if offline-first or peer-to-peer matters more, I'd use a sequence CRDT like Yjs and still relay through a server for persistence.

head: Failure
Impact
Mitigation
rows: Lease expires, new owner loads snapshot + op log tail; clients resend unacked ops
Two servers think they own a doc
Lease with fencing token on op-log appends (conditional on last rev)
Rebase in chunks; CRDT merge; warn on conflicts
Viewers read-only via fan-out tier; editors capped

items.title: Wrap-up
items.text: Snapshot cadence, viral docs, convergence tests.

items.a: Snapshots plus op log; group ops by author and time into named revisions; restore = new ops that recreate the old state.
Ops marked as suggestions in a separate layer, rendered differently, accepted by converting to normal ops.
Locks hurt the live-collaboration experience and fail badly offline; OT/CRDT avoid them.
Fuzz testing: random concurrent ops from simulated clients, assert all replicas end identical.

items: Apply locally first, send op with base revision.
One session server per doc orders ops.
OT: transform concurrent ops; CRDT: merge by unique IDs.
Op log + snapshots = history and recovery.
Lease + fencing to avoid two owners.
Cursors and comments are transformed positions.
